abstract.title: Significance
abstract.p: Lions and tigers were widespread apex predators during the Late Pleistocene and integral components of East Asian megafauna. Cave lions predominantly inhabited northern Eurasia, whereas tigers were distributed farther south. The boundary between their ranges extended across Eurasia and shifted with climatic fluctuations, such as glacial–interglacial oscillations. Our findings challenge the prevailing view that tigers once took refuge in Japan and that cave lion distribution was limited to the Russian Far East and northeast China. These findings provide evidence that lions, rather than tigers, colonized the Japanese Archipelago during the Late Pleistocene. This finding extends the known range of cave lions in East Asia and refines our understanding of how far south the lion–tiger transition belt shifted during this period.

Lions and tigers, as dominant apex predators, likely became competitors when lions expanded from Africa into Eurasia approximately one million years ago (Ma), forming a lion–tiger transition belt from the Middle East through Central Asia to the Russian Far East. At the easternmost edge of this zone, the Japanese Archipelago has long been considered a Late Pleistocene tiger refugium, supported by large felid subfossils traditionally attributed to tigers (Panthera tigris), though their taxonomic identity remained unresolved. To clarify the origin, evolutionary history, and biogeography of Japan’s Pleistocene felids, we analyzed 26 ancient specimens previously assumed to be tigers. Using mitochondrial and nuclear genome hybridization capture and sequencing, paleoproteomics, Bayesian molecular dating, and radiocarbon dating, we found that all ancient Japanese “tiger” remains yielding molecular data were, unexpectedly, cave lions (Panthera spelaea). One specimen from Yamaguchi Prefecture, western Japan, was radiocarbon dated to 36,000-34,891 cal. BP. These cave lions likely dispersed to the Japanese Archipelago between ~72.7 and 37.5 thousand years ago (ka), when a land bridge connected northern Japan to the mainland during the Last Glacial Period. Our findings challenge the long-held view that tigers once took refuge in Japan, showing instead that cave lions were widespread in northeast Asia during this period and were the Panthera lineage that colonized Japan, reaching even its southwestern regions despite habitats previously thought to favor tigers.

body.p: Both the lion and tiger monophyletic species complexes are thought to have emerged by the Plio–Pleistocene boundary (ca. 2.6 million years ago, Ma) (1–11), although their initial divergence from their closest sister taxa may have occurred during the early to mid-Pliocene (ca. 5.3 to 3.0 Ma) (12–15). In this study, we use the term “lion” to refer to the entire monophyletic lineage encompassing its only surviving species, the modern lion (Panthera leo), as well as extinct species including the Middle Pleistocene European lion (P. fossilis), the Late Pleistocene cave lion (P. spelaea), and the Late Pleistocene American lion (P. atrox) (estimated coalescence time among these species: 0.5 to 1.9 Ma) (2, 6). Similarly, “tiger” refers to the monophyletic lineage that once included multiple species but today is represented solely by the modern tiger (P. tigris).

As dominant apex predators, lions and tigers likely shaped the evolutionary pathways of other sympatric carnivores through both direct and indirect competition, and influenced herbivore populations through predation, since they emerged approximately 2 Ma (1, 8, 9, 16–18). Later, lions and tigers may have become significant competitors to one another, when lions dispersed out of Africa around 1 Ma and began expanding their range across Eurasia (1, 3, 19, 20). Today, however, their geographic ranges no longer overlap, due to extensive contractions that occurred across southwest Eurasia by the early 20th century, driven by anthropogenic activities (21, 22). The closest existing populations are now more than 300 km apart in India: The eastmost population of Asian lions is confined to the Gir Forest in Gujarat, while the westmost population of Indian tigers occurs around Yawal Wildlife Sanctuary in Maharashtra (23).

In contrast, during the Late Pleistocene (ca. 129 to 11.7 thousand years ago, ka), range overlap and interactions between lions and tigers may have occurred more frequently along a transition zone stretching across Eurasia, from the Middle East through Central Asia to the Russian Far East (1, 2, 16, 24–29). We refer to this zone as the “lion–tiger transition belt.” Detailed knowledge of the spatial and temporal distribution of lions and tigers during the Late Pleistocene is essential for understanding their evolutionary histories and ecological roles, particularly in relation to sympatric carnivores and herbivores. However, significant knowledge gaps remain, not least due to the scarcity of data from eastern Eurasia compared to the more thoroughly studied regions of western Eurasia and North America (24, 26, 27, 30–33).

One unresolved issue concerns the taxonomic identification of Pleistocene Panthera species from the Japanese Archipelago. Periodic land connections between the archipelago and the Asian mainland, resulting from lowered sea levels during glacial periods, enabled the migration of continental fauna to Japan (Fig. 1) (34–37). Subfossil remains of large felids belonging to the genus Panthera have been recovered in Japan from stratigraphic layers corresponding to the Middle and Late Pleistocene. Initially, these were attributed to Panthera youngi, P. tigris, or a smaller form tentatively identified as Panthera cf. pardus (leopard) (38–40). However, Hemmer later proposed, based on morphological analysis, that these remains represented tigers (41), a view that has generally been accepted by subsequent authors despite the inherent limitations of species-level identification based on morphology alone (42–44).

caption.p: Map of the Japanese Archipelago (based on the ETOPO Global Relief Model) showing known Japanese “tiger” excavation sites. Gray dots mark locations where putative Japanese tiger specimens were found, but no genomic data were obtained. Red dots mark sites where genomic data were recovered: 1–Shiriya-Zaki, Aomori (mtDNA), 2–Hamamatsu, Shizuoka (mtDNA), and 3–Mine, Yamaguchi (mtDNA and nuclear genome). Arrows indicate two potential migration routes between the continent and the Japanese Archipelago during period when land bridges were present. Dark green shading shows land areas exposed by a ~120 m sea-level drop during cold climatic periods (45, 46).

graphic.alt-text: Map of the Japanese Archipelago showing "tiger" excavation sites, with and without genomic data, and migration routes between the continent and Japan.

body.p: Habitat modeling suggests that the southwestern Japanese Archipelago provided some of the most suitable habitats for tigers in East Asia during the cooler periods of the Late Pleistocene (11, 16, 28, 29). Accordingly, the archipelago may have supported—or served as a key refugium for—resident tiger populations. If this were the case, the Japanese Archipelago could have played a significant role in the evolution and expansion of tigers in East Asia. However, its geographic position at the eastern edge of the lion–tiger transition belt complicates this assumption. During the Late Pleistocene, cave lions appear to have been present in the southeast Russian Far East, northeastern China, and the northern Korean Peninsula (47–50). This raises important questions about which Panthera species migrated to Japan. Yet, the possibility that lions once inhabited the Japanese Archipelago has not been seriously considered, largely due to the current absence of lions from East Asia, despite the lack of positive species-level identification of the Japanese “tiger” remains.

To address this knowledge gap and specifically determine whether the Pleistocene “tigers” of the Japanese Archipelago were indeed lions or tigers, we analyzed 26 subfossil specimens of large felids from the region (SI Appendix, Table S1). Despite the challenges posed by extremely low endogenous DNA in poorly preserved ancient specimens, we successfully resolved species identities using an integrated approach combining radiocarbon dating, paleogenomics, and paleoproteomics. Our analyses leveraged on data from five complete mitochondrial and one partial nuclear genome obtained via hybridization capture enrichment, alongside ancient proteome data that enabled the profiling of species-specific amino acid variants. The data were analyzed in the context of Panthera phylogeny and population genetic structure, incorporating previously published ancient and modern genomes. We also used direct radiocarbon dating and phylogeny-based molecular clock estimation, to reconstruct the faunal dispersal chronology between mainland Asia and the Japanese Archipelago. Our results revealed the unexpected finding that cave lions, rather than tigers, inhabited the Japanese Archipelago during the Late Pleistocene, thereby refining our understanding of how far south the lion–tiger transition belt extended during this period.

sec.title: Species Identification of Ancient Large Felids from Japan.
sec.p: Of the 26 subfossil remains previously described as Japanese tigers, all exhibited extremely low endogenous DNA content (<0.1%) when screened via direct genome resequencing using a next-generation sequencing platform, with the highest yield at 0.095% (SI Appendix, Table S1). Despite this poor preservation, five of eight specimens selected for mitochondrial genome enrichment through hybridization capture recovered nearly complete mitogenomes. These specimens (GMNH0024, GMNH0028, GMNH0031, GMNH0032, GMNH0034), excavated from three major sites on Honshu Island, yielded mitogenome sequencing coverage ranging from 94.33 to 99.43% and sequencing depth from 5.36× to 27.27× (SI Appendix, Table S1), providing sufficient resolution for reliable lineage profiling and phylogenetic analysis.

A mitochondrial DNA phylogeny, incorporating available mitogenome data from other big cat species, particularly those from modern and ancient lions, revealed two major mitochondrial DNA clades from the Late Pleistocene cave lions, namely “spelaea-1” and “spelaea-2” (Fig. 2). The so-called Japanese “tiger’’ specimens form a well-supported monophyletic group nested within “spelaea-1”. Together with “spelaea-2” and other cave lion specimens, these cave lions represent an extinct lineage that was widespread in Eurasia, and sister to the extinct American lion. The modern lion lineage occupies a more basal position within the lion clade. Nevertheless, all lion lineages, both extant and extinct, formed a cohesive species-level clade that is clearly distinct from other Panthera species, such as the tiger and the leopard (P. pardus). These phylogenetic clustering patterns strongly support the identification of the Japanese big cat specimens as cave lions, rather than tigers as previously designated. However, given the uncertainty as to what the biomolecular preservation in the sample would allow as well as the documented cases of mitochondrial introgression among closely related felid species which can obscure species identification (12, 15), we elected to address this question using two additional approaches, nuclear DNA analysis and paleoproteomics.

caption.p: Bayesian time tree based on 15,476-bp aligned mitogenome sequences (excluding the control region) from five Japanese “tiger” specimens and 53 published mitogenomes of Panthera species or lineages: modern lion (Panthera leo), cave lion (P. spelaea), American lion (P. atrox), tiger (P. tigris), leopard (P. pardus), and mainland clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa). Numbers on the nodes are Bayesian posterior probabilities, and bootstrap values for maximum likelihood, neighbor joining, and maximum parsimony methods. Hyphens indicate unsupported monophyly under the corresponding method, and asterisks stand for “1.0/100/100/100.” Coalescent times of two important nodes are labeled in red. Two Eastern Beringian clades in cave lions (spelaea-1 and spelaea-2) (51) are highlighted.

graphic.alt-text: Bayesian time tree of mitogenome sequences from Japanese "tiger" specimens, ancient and modern lions, tigers, leopards, and mainland clouded leopards.

sec.p: We designed a targeted nuclear genome capture array to recover single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) selected computationally for their power to distinguish between tiger and lion lineages (SI Appendix, Fig. S1 and Table S2). Using this SNP-based target enrichment approach, we retrieved data from 5,075 genomic loci (SI Appendix, Tables S1 and S3) from the best-preserved specimen, GMNH0031, a ~35,000-y-old sample that was excavated from Mine, Yamaguchi Prefecture, near the southwestern end of Honshu Island (site 3, Fig. 1). Principal component analysis (PCA) of nuclear genomic data, including tigers, modern lions, and cave lions, confirmed the results of the mtDNA analysis that the Japanese tiger was neither a tiger nor a modern lion, but a cave lion (Fig. 3). PC1 accounted for 38.1% of the total variance and separated lion lineages (modern and ancient) from tigers, while PC2 explained 17.1% of the variance and distinguished modern lions from cave lions. Notably, GMNH0031 was indistinguishable from other cave lions along both axes, providing nuclear genomic evidence that the Japanese “tiger” specimen represents a cave lion, rather than a case of matrilineal introgression.

caption.p: Principal component analysis (PCA) based on 5,071 SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) from a targeted nuclear genome capture array used to assess the identity of the Japanese “tiger” specimen GMNH0031. PC1 (38.1% variance) separates all lion lineages (modern and ancient) from tigers, whereas PC2 (17.1% variance) distinguishes modern lions from cave lions. GMNH0031, represented by two duplicate Illumina libraries, clusters with known cave lions on both PC1 and PC2, confirming its cave lion affinity.

graphic.alt-text: Scatter plot showing modern lions, tigers, cave lions, and the Japanese "tiger" along principal components 1 and 2.

sec.p: Paleoproteomic analysis using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) was conducted to assess species-specific amino acid variants in the Japanese “tiger” remains. Proteomic profiling of specimen GMNH0031 confidently yielded 19 endogenous proteins, each supported by more than two unique peptides, spanning over 2,000 amino acid residues. Within these sequenced protein regions, a diagnostic single amino acid variant distinguishing a lion from a tiger was identified in alpha-2-HS-glycoprotein (AHSG) (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 and Table S4). Specifically, the 84th position of AHSG is methionine in the tiger reference proteome (NCBI accession number: XP_007083656.1), but leucine in the lion reference (XP_042811571.1). GMNH0031 was found to carry leucine at this position, suggesting a closer affinity to lions than to tigers. This variant was further validated through a proteomic analysis of modern zoo specimens, confirming methionine in tiger and leucine in lion (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 and Table S4). Deamidation rates of glutamine and asparagine, which are typically higher in ancient bone materials (52), were 72.3 to 90.5% and 88.4 to 97.0%, respectively, in GMNH0031, compared to much lower rates in modern zoo specimens (2.0 to 2.5% and 41.1 to 48.0%). These results support the authenticity of the recovered ancient proteomic data (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 and Table S5).

In summary, paleogenomic analyses utilizing targeted capture enrichment and sequencing of both mitochondrial and nuclear genomes, alongside the paleoproteomic identification of a species-specific amino acid variant, conclusively demonstrated that the subfossil remains from which data could be generated were not tigers, but rather cave lions. This provides definitive species identification of extinct large felids from the Late Pleistocene Japanese Archipelago. The frequent warm and humid climate, coupled with the widespread presence of acidic volcanic ash soils throughout the archipelago during the Pleistocene, has rendered the region largely unsuitable for long-term biomolecular preservation. These environmental conditions have posed substantial challenges for ancient DNA recovery and broader efforts to reconstruct prehistoric faunal assemblage (37, 53). The successful retrieval of both paleogenomic and paleoproteomic data from large felid remains in this study therefore marks a notable achievement in overcoming these long-standing barriers.

sec.title: Radiocarbon Dating and Molecular Dating of Ancient Cave Lions from Japan.
sec.p: Mitochondrial DNA phylogenetic analysis indicates that the identified cave lion specimens from Japan are most closely related to cave lions from northwest Canada and Alaska belonging to the “spelaea-1” clade, as defined by Salis et al. (51) (Genbank accession numbers: KX2585451.1, OK512987.1, OK512985.1, OK512984.1) (Fig. 2). Together with closely related haplotypes from eastern Siberia (OK513001.1 and OK513003.1), these lineages form a well-supported monophyletic haplogroup, which we here refer to as “spelaea-1”. This group appears to have become extinct in both Eurasia and eastern Beringia by the onset of Marine Isotope Stage 2 (MIS 2, ca. 29 to 14 ka). The youngest known radiocarbon dates for this lineage are 29,860 ± 210 BP in eastern Beringia, and 54,100 ± 1,800 BP in Eurasia (calibrated to 54,556 cal. BP) (51, 54). The “spelaea-1” group was eventually replaced across both Eurasia and Beringia by “spelaea-2” which was a monophyletic haplogroup (51) likely originated in Eurasia before dispersing eastward into Beringia.

Radiocarbon dating of one cave lion specimen (GMNH0031) from Yamaguchi Prefecture, Japan (site 3 in Fig. 1) yielded an age of 31,060 ± 190 BP (95.4% HPD: 36,000 to 34,891 cal. BP) (SI Appendix, Table S1). Four additional Japanese specimens, dated using Bayesian tip-dating of complete mitochondrial genome sequences, fall within a range of ca. 28.7 to 34.9 ka (SI Appendix, Table S1). Notably, another contemporaneous Japanese subfossil specimen previously identified as “tiger” or “leopard” was radiocarbon-dated to 17,910 ± 70 BP (20,950-21,630 cal. BP) (55, 56). These dates suggest that “spelaea-1” members persisted in the Japanese Archipelago for at least 20,000 y after their extinction in Eurasia, and potentially more than 10,000 y after their final disappearance from eastern Beringia, if the more recent Japanese subfossil mentioned above is genetically confirmed to belong to “spelaea-1”.

This extended survival of cave lions may reflect Japan’s unique paleogeographic history. Periods of relative isolation, punctuated by episodic land connections to the continent, have historically enabled the persistence of relict populations, such as the Japanese wolf (Canis lupus), which survived well into the Holocene, after their continental counterpart population went extinct (57). Similarly, biogeographic isolation in the archipelago may have driven lineage-specific adaptations, as seen in the endemic Plio-Pleistocene elephants of the genus Stegodon (35). Our results indicate that a relict population of cave lions from the “spelaea-1” group survived in the Japanese Archipelago well beyond their extinction elsewhere in northern Eurasia. Future research should investigate whether this group was entirely restricted to the Japanese Archipelago in the Late Pleistocene, or whether it may also have persisted in parts of southeastern Siberia or northern China that are near the archipelago, while northeastern Siberia was dominated by the “spelaea-2” group (58).

sec.title: Arrival and Colonization of Cave Lions in Japan during the Late Pleistocene.
sec.p: The Japanese Archipelago has remained largely isolated for the past ~1 My, with intermittent land connections to the Asian mainland occurring during periods of lowered sea levels. These land bridges formed at the southwestern and northern extremities of the crescent-shaped archipelago—around 35°N and 50°N latitude, respectively—but not necessarily at the same time. In the southwest, connections are thought to have emerged during MIS 16 (ca. 650 ka) and MIS 12 (ca. 430 ka), while in the north, links occurred during MIS 4 to 2 (the Last Glacial Period, ca. 115 to 11 ka) (34–37). These brief, but critical, land corridors played a major role in shaping the region’s biogeographic and faunal history (Fig. 1) (34, 37, 56, 59). The southwestern route likely linked the archipelago to temperate biomes of the Asian mainland, while the northern connection, 15° further north, opened pathways to sub-Arctic ecosystems, allowing species from distinct ecological biomes to migrate into the archipelago (35, 37, 56).

Fossil records showed that lions dispersed out of Africa around 1 Ma and reached Europe by ca. 750 to 700 ka (19, 60–62). Under favorable conditions without natural barriers, lions are capable of long-distance travel, covering up to 80 km in just 2 d (1). Although the precise timing of their arrival in eastern Siberia and East Asia remains unclear, lion remains have been discovered in Alaskan deposits from the Illinoian and Wisconsin glaciations (ca. 191 to 11 ka) (1, 24, 26). These findings imply that lions had already reached eastern Siberia prior to crossing into North America. It is thus reasonable to infer that lions were present in eastern Siberia and potentially East Asia, during the glacial periods of MIS 4 to 2 (ca. 115 to 11 ka) when the north land bridge intermittently connected the continent with the Japanese Archipelago. Paleogenomic analyses suggest that at least three waves of lion dispersal into North America occurred during this timeframe, involving the P. atrox clade and two cave lion lineages, spelaea-1 and spelaea-2 (51).

Little is known about the spatial or temporal presence of these lion clades in southeastern Siberia, the closest continental region to the Japanese Archipelago. Other carnivores, such as wolves and brown bears (Ursus arctos), show archeological and genetic evidence of multiple colonization waves, and/or admixture events within the archipelago (37, 57, 63), raising the possibility of a similar scenario for lions. Our paleogenomic data of five ancient big cat mitogenomes from three sites on Honshu Island revealed a monophyletic haplogroup closely associated with the spelaea-1 group (Fig. 4). The estimated coalescence time among the Japanese cave lions was ca. 37.5 ka (95% HPD: 35.8 to 39.6 ka), with a divergence from the broader spelaea-1 clade around ca. 72.7 ka (95% HPD: 67.1 to 78.2 ka). These findings suggest that lions likely colonized the Japanese Archipelago between ca. 72.7 and 37.5 Ka, coinciding with cold glacial phases of MIS 4 to 2, when the northern land bridge was periodically accessible (Fig. 1).

caption.p: Maps showing the possible distributions of lions and tigers in eastern Eurasia and Alaska during different Marine Isotope Stages (MIS) of the Late Pleistocene, constructed using the ETOPO Global Relief Model (64). (A) MIS-6 (ca. 191 to 130 ka: cold period) during which lions of the atrox clade migrated from Eurasia to Alaska. (B) MIS-4 (ca. 71 to 57 ka: cold period) during which lions of “spelaea-1” migrated from Eurasia to Alaska, where the previous atrox clade was still present, and this spelaea-1 group also migrated to the Japanese Archipelago. (C) MIS-2 (ca. 29 to 11 ka: cold period) during which lions of “spelaea-2” migrated from Eurasia to Alaska, where the previous atrox clade and spelaea-1 group were absent, but the spelaea-1 group persisted in the Japanese Archipelago. (D) Present time (MIS-1: warm period) where lions became extinct in the region, and tigers expanded their distribution northward to colonize the southeast Russian Far East. The dark green areas indicate the land surface exposed by sea-level declines of 120 m during MIS-6 (A) and MIS-2 (C), and 95 m during MIS-4 (B). Question marks “?” on panels (A and C) denote uncertainty in species designations from those regions and in the position of the likely lion–tiger transition belt.

graphic.alt-text: Four maps showing lion and tiger distributions in eastern Eurasia and Alaska during Marine Isotope Stages 6, 4, 2, and 1.

sec.p: This timeframe also corresponds with the arrival of other sub-Arctic megafauna into Japan during the Last Glacial Period, including woolly mammoths (Mammuthus primigenius), bison (Bison sp.), elk (Alces alces), lynx (Lynx sp.), reindeer (Rangifer tarandus), and possibly aurochs (Bos primigenius) (36, 43, 56, 65, 66). Fossil evidence indicates that lynx, elk, and, based on our findings, cave lions reached central Japan. Notably, only lynx and cave lions extended further into the southwestern part of the archipelago. These species likely dispersed along ecological corridors that transitioned from open coniferous woodland and grassland in the north, through temperate coniferous forests, to temperate broadleaf forests in the south (43, 56, 65, 67).

sec.title: Cave Lions in the Tiger Habitat of the Japanese Archipelago.
sec.p: The southwestern part of the Japanese Archipelago both today and during the Late Pleistocene provides an ecologically favorable habitat for tigers (11, 28, 29). Thus, had tigers been present, it is reasonable to speculate that they may have competitively excluded lions from colonizing the region. However, our results do not confirm the presence of tigers on the archipelago during the Late Pleistocene.

Both the fossil record and molecular phylogenies suggest that Late Pleistocene tigers of East Asia expanded their range northward into the southeastern Russian Far East during warmer interglacial periods, and retreated southward during cooler phases, when cave lions occupied these northern regions instead (11, 49, 68). This pattern supports the hypothesis that lions, rather than tigers, were more likely to have crossed into the Japanese Archipelago via land bridges that formed during colder glacial periods. Oscillations of the lion–tiger transition were primarily influenced by climate-driven shifts in each species’ preferred habitats, although the likely group-living lion’s potential advantage over the solitary tiger in direct competition may also have shaped the belt’s position (1). During this time, wolves, brown bears, and Asian black bears (Ursus thibetanus) were also present on the archipelago (37, 56, 63), alongside early human populations, which arrived in Japan by ca. 40 to 35 ka (53, 69). Our findings demonstrate that cave lions coexisted with these large carnivorous and hypocarnivorous mammals, forming an integral part of the Late Pleistocene ecosystem in the Japanese Archipelago.

sec.title: The Extinction of Pleistocene Cave Lions in Japan.
sec.p: Most megafauna on the Japanese Archipelago went extinct by the end of the Pleistocene, including cave lions (the youngest large felid fossil, presumably of a cave lion based on this study, dated to 17,910 ± 70 BP or 20,950 to 21,630 cal. BP), woolly mammoth (19,530 ± 80 BP), Naumann’s elephant (Palaeoloxodon naumanni) (23,600 ± 130 BP), bison (17,900 ± 90 BP), and giant deer (Sinomegaceros yabei) (40,560 ± 1,500 BP) (55, 56). Brown bears also disappeared from much of the archipelago shortly after ca. 20 ka, persisting only on Hokkaido, whereas the Asian black bear survived and continues to inhabit parts of Japan today (37). The lynx persisted until several thousand years ago, and the wolf survived into the 20th century (63, 65).

The causes of these extinctions remain debated. Iwase et al. (56) argue that climatic and environment shifts were the primary drivers, as the timing of extinction events closely aligns with major climate changes, rather than with evidence of human overhunting. In contrast, Kondo et al. (67) suggest that archaeological records indicate humans hunted large mammals such as Naumann’s elephants, implying anthropogenic impacts cannot be ruled out. Hasegawa et al. (65) note the temporal overlap between the arrival of humans and rapid climate change, complicating efforts to disentangle their respective roles in megafauna extinctions on the Japanese Archipelago. These uncertainties have long obscured our understanding of Late Pleistocene faunal histories in Japan.

Our findings provide evidence that it was cave lions, not tigers, that colonized the Japanese Archipelago via land connections with northeast Asia. Despite habitats that may have appeared more favorable for tigers during the LGM, it was cave lions that likely dispersed widely across the archipelago, reaching even its southwestern extent. This finding extends the known range of cave lions in East Asia and sheds light on the biogeographical patterns of the lion–tiger transition during the Late Pleistocene. Future reexamination of lion and tiger subfossil remains across mid-latitude Eurasia will be essential for clarifying species range dynamics and resolving the oscillations of the lion–tiger belt.

sec.title: Ancient Specimen Sampling and Radiocarbon Dating.
sec.p: All specimens in this study were obtained through archaeological excavations in collaboration with museum curators. Small bone or tooth fragments (approximately 10 × 10 × 5 mm) were collected from 26 subfossil specimens of putative tigers recovered from four excavation sites in northern, central, and western Honshu Island, Japan (Fig. 1 and SI Appendix, Table S1).

DNA extraction was performed in a dedicated ancient DNA facility at the School of Life Sciences, Peking University, Beijing, China, following established protocols (70), with a slight modification including a predigestion step to reduce external DNA contamination (11, 71). Double-stranded next-generation sequencing libraries were prepared using the Blunt-End Single-Tube (BEST) protocol (72) and sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 platform at Novogene (Novogene Corporation Inc., Beijing), generating approximately 3 Gb of raw data per sample. Endogenous DNA content was assessed by calculating the proportion of nucleotides mapped to the tiger reference genome (73).

A bone fragment from an ulna of sample GMNH0031 (originally labeled as “宇伊”, SI Appendix, Table S1) was selected for accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS)-14C radiocarbon dating at Beta Analytic, Inc. (Miami, FL, USA). Calibration of conventional radiocarbon age to calendar years was performed based on the IntCal20 atmospheric curve (74) using OxCal v4.4 (75).

sec.title: Mitochondrial Genome Capture and Sequencing.
sec.p: Eight samples with endogenous DNA content exceeding 0.01% were selected for mitogenome capture enrichment using the “myBaits Expert Mito” kit specifically designed for the tiger (Daicel Arbor Biosciences, Ann Arbor, MI, USA). Hybridization was carried out at 55 °C for 48 h, following the manufacturer’s instructions.

Paired-end reads were generated on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform at Novogene. AdapterRemoval v2.2.2 (76) was used to trim adapters and collapse overlapping reads derived from the same short insert fragments. The reads were further filtered and trimmed using Cutadapt v3.2 (77). Reads with a quality score below 15 were removed. Five base pairs were trimmed from both ends and reads shorter than 25 bp or containing more than 10% ambiguous bases (N) were discarded. The resulting clean reads were mapped to mitochondrial reference genomes of cave lion, modern lion, and tiger (GenBank accession numbers: KX258452.1 and OK512998.1, NC_028302.1, and KP202268.1) using BWA-backtrack algorithm implemented in BWA v0.7.17 (78). Mapping parameters were set as follows: maximum gap open = 2, maximum fraction of missing alignment = 0.01, and seeding was disabled. Mapped reads were processed with SAMtools v1.11 (79) to sort alignments, remove PCR duplicates, and filter out reads with mapping quality below 30.

We quantified cytosine deamination, which is a hallmark of postmortem DNA damage, using mapDamage2 (80). The elevated frequency of terminal C-to-T and G-to-A substitutions provided robust evidence for the presence of authentic endogenous ancient DNA.

sec.title: Mitochondrial Phylogenomic Analysis and Bayesian Tip Dating.
sec.p: Among the four mitochondrial reference genomes from lions or tigers, the highest number of reads were mapped to the cave lion mitogenome (GenBank accession number: KX258452.1) (SI Appendix, Table S6). Consequently, this reference was used for subsequent analyses. Mitochondrial genomes were assembled from mapped reads using ANGSD (81). The consensus sequence was generated by calling the most frequent base at each site, while positions with less than 3× coverage or lacking ≥2/3 base agreement were masked with “N.”

Consensus mitochondrial genome sequences of the Japanese tiger samples were aligned with 53 published mitogenomes, including two mainland clouded leopards (Neofelis nebulosa), six modern tigers, two leopards (Panthera pardus), two modern lions, 11 American lions, and 30 cave lions (SI Appendix, Table S7), using MAFFT v7.505 (82) with default setting. The best-fitting nucleotide substitution model was determined using jModelTest v2.1.7 (83), based on Akaike Information Criterion (AIC).

Bayesian tip-dating in the mitochondrial phylogenetic framework was conducted using BEAST v2.6.6 (84) (SI Appendix, Table S1). Twenty-one cave lions and seven American lions with previously published radiocarbon dates (SI Appendix, Table S7) were used to calibrate the molecular clock. The temporal signal of the dataset was assessed using TempEst v1.5.3 (85), and individuals showing anomalous signals—characterized by regression ancestor race lines nearly parallel to the x-axis, indicating incorrect dating—were excluded from the analysis. Tip-dating was performed using a coalescent constant population prior and a strict molecular clock model. The clock rate was estimated under a uniform prior with bounds set between 0 and 500,000, following Salis et al. (51).

A Bayesian mitochondrial DNA phylogenetic tree was constructed using BEAST v2.6.6 under Bayesian Skyline model (86). The Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) was run for 20,000,000 generations, with genealogies sampled every 1,000 steps. Tracer v1.7.1 (87) was used to assess convergence and ensure adequate effective sample sizes (ESS). A maximum clade credibility tree was then generated after discarding the first 10% of samples as burn-in. For comparison, a best-scoring maximum likelihood (ML) tree was constructed using RAXML v8.2.12 (88), employing rapid bootstrap analysis with 100 replicates. Additionally, maximum parsimony (MP) and neighbor-joining (NJ) phylogenies were inferred using PAUP v4.0a (89), each with 100 bootstrap replicates.

sec.title: Targeted Nuclear Genome Capture and Sequencing.
sec.p: To investigate the nuclear genomic ancestry of ancient felid remains from Japan, we performed targeted nuclear DNA capture and sequencing on sample GMNH0031. The hybridization capture enrichment assay was designed to target SNPs that distinguish among key Panthera species (i.e., tiger, extant lion, and extinct cave lion), using nuclear genome data from two published cave lions, seven modern lions, and eight modern tigers (SI Appendix, Table S2) (6, 10, 73, 90). Sequences were mapped to the domestic cat Felis_catus_9.0 reference genome (RefSeq assembly GCF_000181335.4) (91) using PALEOMIX v1.2.13.2 (92), and genotype likelihoods were estimated with ANGSD (81). Variable sites were retained if the minor allele frequency was ≥0.05 and missing data occurred in less than half of the samples. To reduce potential biases from ancient DNA damage, we removed transitions and excluded sites within repetitive elements, based on the UCSC Genome Browser annotations for Felis_catus_9.0.

Mappability scores were calculated with GenMap v1.3.0 (93) and only sites with a score of 1 were retained. To minimize the influence of nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (numts), we screened the genomes for potential numts using mitochondrial sequences from cave lion (KX258452.1), modern lion (KP202262.1), and modern tiger (KP202268.1), following previously established protocols (10, 11). SNPs within putative numt regions were excluded, resulting in a filtered set of 2,846,194 high-confidence variable sites. From these, one SNP per 100 kb window was selected, and a final set of 20,000 SNPs was then randomly chosen for probe design.

Prior to finalizing the capture probe set, we computationally validated whether the selected SNPs could effectively resolve species identities through principal component analysis (PCA) and phylogenetic reconstruction. PCA was conducted using PCAngsd v1.11 (94), and phylogenetic trees were reconstructed with ngsDist based on pairwise genetic distance and 100 bootstrap replicates. Capture probes were synthesized by Daciel Arbor Biosciences (Ann Arbor, MI, USA).

Duplicate Illumina sequencing libraries of sample GMNH0031, prepared independently in ancient DNA laboratories at the Globe Institute, University of Copenhagen (GMNH0031-1 based on the Santa Cruz Reaction, a single-stranded DNA library preparation method optimized for ancient and degraded DNA) (95) and School of Life Sciences, Peking University (GMNH0031-2 based on the “Blunt-End Single-Tube” or BEST protocol) (72), were then submitted to Daciel Arbor Biosciences for two rounds of hybridization-based target enrichment. The enriched libraries were sequenced on an Illumina Novaseq 6000 platform at Novogene, generating approximately 140 and 180 million 150 bp paired-end reads per library, respectively (SI Appendix, Table S3).

Captured sequencing data were processed using the same mapping and variant-calling pipeline employed during probe design. From the enriched libraries, 5,075 loci with sufficient genotype likelihoods were recovered. PCA and phylogenetic analyses were repeated on these loci using the same parameters applied during the validation phase. All scripts and pipelines used for probe design, validation, and downstream analysis are available at https://github.com/xinsun1/Tiger-Lion_AIMs/blob/main/AIMs_pipeline.md.

sec.title: Paleoproteomic Analysis.
sec.p: Paleoproteomic analysis was conducted to assess whether the endogenous protein sequence recovered from ancient specimens contained diagnostic variants characteristic of lions or tigers. Protein extraction from GMNH0031 was conducted in a dedicated ancient biomolecule facility at the Globe Institute, University of Copenhagen, using two established methods. First, a filter-aided protocol was applied to 20 mg of bone, involving decalcification with 0.5 M EDTA for two days, and filtering the supernatant through a molecular weight cutoff filter (Amicon 3000 Da), in order to buffer exchange into 300 μL 2 M guanidine hydrochloride (Gu), 10 mM tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP), and 20 mM 2-chloroacetamide (CAA). The same buffer and amount was added to the remaining sample pellet from decalcification and, in parallel, these two samples were subjected to denaturation, reduction, and alkylation at 80 °C for 2 to 4 h followed by sequential digestion with 0.2 μg Lys-C (1.5 h at 37 °C) and 0.8 μg trypsin (overnight at 37 °C) after dilution of Gu to 0.6 M (96, 97). The second method was a digestion-free protocol in which 5.5 mg of bone was dissolved in 10% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) at 4 °C for 2 d (98, 99). Blank controls were processed in parallel to monitor for potential exogenous contamination.

To minimize potential biases arising from annotation or translation errors in public protein databases, we analyzed bone proteomes from taxonomically verified lions and tigers. Proteins were extracted from modern samples of a lion (NHMD-CN-887) and a tiger (NHMD-CN-1021) kept at the Natural History Museum of Denmark. Approximately 20 mg of bone powder from each specimen was incubated in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate (ambic) at 65 °C for 1 h. Protein concentration was measured using a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (100), and two 20 μg aliquots were taken for digestion. For samples subjected to elastase digestion, ambic was evaporated, and the sample was resuspended in 50 mM Tris-HCl, followed by overnight digestion at 37 °C with either 0.4 μg elastase or trypsin.

The resultant peptide solutions from all methods were purified using in-house-made reversed-phase C18 StageTips composed of two stacked C18 membranes (101). Peptides were eluted from the StageTips and injected into a liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) at the Center for Protein Research, University of Copenhagen. Separation was performed on a 15 cm column packed with 1.9 μm C18 beads using an EASY-nLC 1200 system (Proxeon, Odense, Denmark) coupled to a Q-Exactive HF-X (Thermo Scientific, Germany; Trypsin digested ancient samples) or an Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, Germany; all other samples) with a 77-min gradient, following previously described parameters (97, 102).

Mass spectrometry raw files were processed using a two-step database search strategy to refine species-specific protein identification. First, trypsin-digested fractions from GMNH0031 were searched in MaxQuant v2.6.3.0 using a “specific” digestion mode against a merged database comprising complete modern lion and tiger proteomes downloaded from NCBI (May 2025; SI Appendix, Table S8). Similarly, the reference datasets from modern lion and tiger bones were searched against their respective species-specific databases (SI Appendix, Tables S9 and S10). In the second step, a reduced protein database was constructed, consisting of lion and tiger proteins (n = 70) identified in the first search with at least two razor and unique peptides. For each identified protein, homologous sequences from both species were included, even if the protein was detected in only one species. All ancient and modern fractions were then searched using an “unspecific” digestion mode against this reduced database. The results of the second search formed the basis for downstream analysis (SI Appendix, Tables S11–S13).

Panthera protein sequences identified in GMNH0031 were aligned using MAFFT (103) (SI Appendix, Table S11). MS2 spectra corresponding to variant positions identified in the second MaxQuant search were manually examined to evaluate whether species identification was supported by mass spectrometry data. Deamidation rates, as indicators of protein preservation, were calculated using a Python script following Mackie et al. (104). The R scripts used for protein sequence reconstruction and visualization were deposited in the Zenodo repository (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.15725677).
